summary:
RegiÃ³n de Tarapacá stands under Chile's national legal framework. Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019: adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery, people aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and those under 14 cannot use the law although the statute recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, and that ruling applies only to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance in the criminal code. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. Chile's Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.

The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, while the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents.

Restrictive proposals are active but non-binding. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

Transphobic violence remains documented under this framework. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime, with the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessing. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

The controlling risk for a transgender visitor to Tarapacá is judicial rather than statutory. In early October 2023 the Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled in whole the trial of Jhonatan Cañon for the 2022 murder of trans woman Yuri Pizarro in Tarapacá, holding that Chile's femicidio offence covers only 'a person biologically female' and so the conviction could not stand as framed. The annulment voided the strongest gendered-violence conviction available and took effect in Tarapacá, where the Iquique court exercises jurisdiction.

Regional incident data point the same direction. Movilh's XXIII annual report, published in March 2025 on 2024 figures, records that Tarapacá held about 2% of nationally documented homo/transphobic cases and ranked among the fastest-rising regions, at +18.18% year-on-year, with growth also recorded at +19.51% in the period tables.
tangentialFactors:
Tarapacá's position on documented anti-LGBT violence is small in absolute share and steep in trajectory. Movilh's 2024 data place the region at roughly 2% of nationally documented homo/transphobic cases, alongside year-on-year growth of 18.18% and a second period figure of 19.51%, which places it among the fastest-rising regions rather than among the highest-volume ones.

The regional pattern diverges from the national statutory position. Chile's statutes recognise gender identity through self-determination, hate-crime aggravation and asylum protection, yet a Tarapacá appellate court used a biological-female reading of femicidio to void a completed murder trial in 2023, leaving the region without the strongest gendered-violence conviction in that case.

National restriction efforts remain advisory at this stage. The CEI 57 report approved by the Chamber of Deputies on 15 May 2025 carries no binding force, and funding decisions that touch trans care have themselves been reversed by the Constitutional Court, as with section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law annulled on 9 January 2025 by seven votes to three.

Chile's regional variation in documented incidents is a national phenomenon rather than a Tarapacá peculiarity, and Movilh's counts measure reported and documented cases, not the full incidence of hostility a visitor may encounter in Iquique or the pampino communes.

Minors aged 14 to 18 apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents; the constitutional ruling of 9 April 2025 on the under-14 wording applies only to the case in which it was brought.

Ministry of Health-run support for trans people continues in medical centres after Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law in November 2025, and the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Circular 7 of June 2024 suggested deferring new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published, while the Medical College stated that physicians may still prescribe.

Residents who face persecution abroad, or who sponsor relatives, may rely on Article 10 of the Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021, which bars expulsion or return to a country where the right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
The consequences of the 5 October 2023 annulment for Jhonatan Cañon are unresolved in the available sources. Whether a retried trial followed, what charges were brought after the femicidio framing was voided, and whether any conviction now stands are not sourced here.

Movilh's two growth figures for Tarapacá, +18.18% year-on-year and +19.51% in the period tables, are reported as stated in the XXIII annual report without confirmation of which time periods each refers to; the discrepancy is not resolved by the inventory.

Whether the Court of Appeals of Iquique's biological-female reading of femicidio has been appealed, upheld by the Supreme Court, or confined to that proceeding is not sourced in this inventory.

Implementation of the Gendarmería de Chile gender-identity protocol at specific establishments in Tarapacá, including Iquique, is not evidenced here, nor is the availability of trans-specific services or facilities within the region.

The practical effect of the 15 May 2025 CEI 57 recommendation on Chilean policy, and of Circular 7 of June 2024 on prescribing practice in Tarapacá, is not sourced; both are recorded as recommendations and guidance rather than binding rules.
